pages.title: About The Ambiguity Project
pages.description: What The Ambiguity Project does and how we do it.
pages.body:
The Ambiguity Project is a 501(c)(3) non-profit helping people, students, businesses, governments, organizations, and schools better recognize, live with, and navigate ambiguity.

We write books, share what we are learning on our blog, and build tools that support people as they confront ambiguity in different situations.

pages.title: Ambiguity Everywhere
pages.description: Ambiguity Everywhere: shaping our lives, society, and the world.
pages.body: All of life’s experiences, from how we learn, to our relationships, to scientific progress, to the economy, to voting, and much more, are ambiguous. *Ambiguity Everywhere* explores these wide-ranging aspects of our world and how experts in each approach and manage ambiguity.

library.title: Radical Uncertainty
library.author: John Kay & Mervyn King
library.coverAlt: Cover of Radical Uncertainty by John Kay & Mervyn King
library.summary: Two economists argue that most of the decisions that matter can't be reduced to probabilities, and that pretending otherwise makes us worse at them.
library.body:
## Why we picked it

Kay and King spent their careers inside institutions that run on forecasts, a former Bank of England governor among them. That makes their central claim land harder: for most important decisions we do not know the odds, and often we don't even know the full list of things that might happen.

## What it gets right

The book separates *resolvable* uncertainty, the kind a coin flip or an actuarial table can handle, from *radical* uncertainty, where the question itself is still fuzzy. Their antidote is a deceptively simple question to ask before any big decision: **"What is going on here?"** Before reaching for a model, build a narrative that makes sense of the situation, then test it.

This is exactly the habit we try to teach. Naming the kind of ambiguity you are facing comes before choosing a tool to deal with it.

## Where it drags

The middle third leans heavily on critiques of economic modelling that will feel familiar to anyone who lived through 2008. Readers outside finance can skim it.

## Who should read it

Anyone who has sat in a meeting where a spreadsheet's false precision ended the conversation too early.
